conclusion: On these 60 hand-labelled prompts, a length-and-keyword rule agreed with the labels 91.7% of the time, cut cost by 32.8% versus always-big under an illustrative price and token model, and took about 0.31 microseconds per decision, but it still sent 3 hard-labelled prompts to the small model.
setup: 60 hand-labelled prompts (42 easy, 18 hard); rule: long>280 chars +1, maths/code/reasoning signals +2 each, big if score>=2; prices per 1M tokens small 0.15/0.6, big 3/15 USD (in/out, assumed illustrative tiers, not dated vendor prices); input tokens = chars/4, output tokens easy 60, hard 500; latency small 250ms+150tok/s, big 700ms+50tok/s; hypothetical escalation: uses true labels, small fails hard-labelled prompt p=0.6, checker detects p=0.8, big always succeeds, checker cost/latency excluded; routing time over 120000 decisions
caveats: Label agreement measures routing against subjective difficulty labels, not answer correctness or which model actually suffices.
Three of 18 hard-labelled prompts were sent to the small model: a 16.7% miss rate within that group, or 5% of all prompts.
The fixed dataset is small and hand-selected; its 70% easy share does not establish the composition of real traffic.
No model answers, live bills, or model response latencies were measured. Prices, token counts, output lengths, and response speeds are assumptions.
The 30 and 6 errors per 1,000 are hypothetical expectations, not observed failures.
Escalation assumes access to true difficulty labels, specified failure and detection probabilities, and a big model that always succeeds. Checker cost and latency are excluded.
The routing benchmark covers local rule execution, not network, gateway, serialization, or end-to-end overhead. Repeated decisions do not increase the number of independently evaluated prompts.
The supplied tail supports arithmetic checks but does not independently validate the implementation or benchmark methodology.
supportedClaims: The rule agreed with hand labels on 55 of 60 prompts: 91.7%.
It sent 43 of 60 prompts (71.7%) to the small model, including 3 hard-labelled prompts; 2 easy-labelled prompts went to the big model.
The printed cost estimates support approximately 32.8% savings using the underlying unrounded figures: $2.923 versus $1.966 per 1,000 requests.
The assumed latency model supports 4,540 ms versus 3,351 ms, approximately 26.2% lower average latency.
The hypothetical error arithmetic is consistent: 3/60 × 0.6 × 1,000 = 30; applying 80% detection leaves 6.
The log reports a routing benchmark averaging 0.31 microseconds per decision over 120,000 decisions.
